$comment: The ONE list of words that mean a string is carrying a credential, read by BOTH halves of this product. It is a build-time source of truth: the server embeds it (CoaiMcp.Core.csproj) and the extension generates a module from it (scripts/generate-credential-words.mjs). NOTHING reads this file at runtime — a published AOT binary and an installed VSIX run where no shared/ directory exists, and a redactor that fell back to an empty list there would put raw credentials into server-notices.jsonl. Both sides fail CLOSED instead.
$why-cases: The corpus BOTH halves answer, and the reason it is here rather than in either suite. Each side used to be checked against its own hand-written table, so a C# splitter that disagreed with the TypeScript one about `requestSig`, `auth-key` or `token2` would leave both suites green while the extension and the server redacted different notices — a secret on disk on one path and not the other. A reviewer named exactly that on this story's plan round. Every case below is asserted by CredentialWordsTests.cs and by credentialWords.test.ts, against the SHIPPED recognisers.
$why-two-lists: They are not one list and must never be merged. A word in `anywhere` matches inside a name, so `client_secret` and a run-together `myapikey` are caught without anything knowing how the name was spelled. A word in `wholePart` matches only a WHOLE part after splitting on separators and camelCase, because matching these three as substrings was a real defect: `author`, `assignee`, `design`, `signal` and `monkey` all matched, so a legitimate endpoint URL was refused and a diagnostic parameter carrying nothing was redacted. A redaction that fires on `?author=octocat` teaches people the mechanism is noise, which is how a real one gets ignored.
